h1: Why Is My Olive Oil Cloudy, With Sediment at the Bottom?
excerpt: A haze in the bottle and a layer at the bottom are three different things wearing one face: cold, olive solids, or an oil that is genuinely finished. Only one of them means throw it out.
keyTakeaway: Cloudiness is almost never a verdict. Cold haze reverses in about an hour on the counter, and sediment in an unfiltered oil is fine olive solids rather than damage, though they shorten the bottle's life. Only the smell decides whether an oil is finished, and a rancid oil can be perfectly clear.

intro: A haze in the bottle and a fine layer at the bottom is the most searched olive oil worry there is, and the answer is almost always that nothing is wrong.
Three separate things get called cloudy, and only one means the oil is finished.

sections.heading: The three things people call cloudy

blocks.text: Cold haze, unfiltered sediment and genuine spoilage look nothing alike once you know what separates them. Haze is temperature, and it undoes itself. Sediment is olive solids that settled out. Spoilage is a change in smell, and a rancid oil can be perfectly clear while a cloudy one is perfectly good.

sections.heading: Cold haze reverses at room temperature

blocks.text: Olive oil is a blend of fats that set at different temperatures, so a bottle below roughly ten degrees clouds, and one at fridge temperature stiffens into soft white lumps. The change is physical, not chemical. About an hour on a Malaysian counter and the bottle pours clear again.

This is also why the fridge test proves nothing. How much an oil hazes in the cold follows the olive variety and the temperature it reached, not whether it is genuine. A bottle that sets is no more real than one that stays clear.

A soft layer at the bottom of a young oil is fine olive solids and a trace of fruit water that were never filtered out. It is normal, not a fault. It does shorten the bottle's life, because those solids carry moisture and slowly ferment, so an unfiltered bottle wants finishing.

items: **Do not shake it back in.** Pour off the clear oil and leave the last centimetre.
**Keep it closed and dark.** Light and air do far more damage than the solids do.
**Finish it sooner.** Roughly two months from opening, as [olive oil shelf life](/blog/olive-oil-shelf-life-how-long-a-bottle-lasts) sets out.

sections.heading: Filtered against unfiltered is a choice, not a fault

blocks.text: Filtering passes the fresh oil through cloth or a fine filter to take the solids out. An unfiltered oil skips that and goes into the bottle hazy and a little fuller in the mouth. Neither is a grade and neither is a defect, and which one a bottle is belongs on its label.

The trade-off is time. Filtered oil stays bright and keeps better; unfiltered shows more of the fresh fruit early and fades sooner. Both meet the same extra virgin standard, set by chemistry and tasting, never by clarity. The range sits on the [products page](/products).

sections.heading: The smell test is the only one that settles it

blocks.text: Pour a spoonful, cup it in your palm for a moment, and smell it. Sound oil smells green — cut grass, fresh olive, a little almond — and catches at the back of the throat. A finished oil smells of wax crayon, putty or stale nuts, or of nothing.

Bitterness and pepper get mistaken for faults constantly, which [why olive oil tastes bitter](/blog/why-does-olive-oil-taste-bitter) goes through properly. Damp cardboard, sour or fermented notes are a different matter.

sections.heading: What a Malaysian kitchen does to the bottle

blocks.text: An air-conditioned kitchen at twenty-four degrees is nowhere near cold enough to haze a bottle, so a cloudy oil here has usually been in the fridge or has solids in it. The fridge is not necessary, and heat is the real enemy: the cupboard beside the hob.
One local wrinkle: a bottle out of the fridge sweats, and those drops run into the neck as you pour. Let it come back to room temperature and dry the outside first.

Cloudy is not a verdict. A cold bottle needs an hour on the counter. A hazy one at room temperature with a layer underneath is unfiltered, and wants finishing. Only the smell tells you an oil is done.

faqs.q: Is cloudy olive oil safe to use?
faqs.a: Almost always, yes. Cold haze reverses on the counter, and unfiltered sediment is normal in a young oil. Cloudiness on its own says nothing about whether an oil is sound; the smell does.

faqs.q: Why is there sediment at the bottom of my olive oil?
faqs.a: Because the oil was bottled without filtering, or with only light filtering, so fine olive solids and a little fruit water settled out over the following weeks. It is normal, and it is not damage.

faqs.q: How long does cloudy olive oil take to clear?
faqs.a: About an hour at room temperature for a haze, and longer for a bottle that has set firm in a fridge. Nothing needs doing beyond leaving it on the counter; never warm it on the hob.

faqs.q: Does olive oil clouding in the fridge prove it is real?
faqs.a: No, and staying clear proves nothing either. How much an oil hazes in the cold follows the olive variety and the temperature it reached, not whether it was blended with something cheaper.

faqs.q: Is unfiltered olive oil better than filtered?
faqs.a: Neither is better. Unfiltered shows more of the fresh fruit early and keeps less well; filtered stays bright and stable for longer. Both can be extra virgin, since the grade is set by chemistry and tasting.

faqs.q: How do I know my olive oil has actually gone off?
faqs.a: Smell it. A finished oil smells of wax crayon, putty or stale nuts, or has lost its aroma entirely, and tastes flat and greasy with no peppery catch at the back of the throat.
